Liverpool vs Manchester United Red Card Decision Overturned
articles.summary: An independent regulatory commission has found that referee Sam Barrott made an error in sending off Manchester United defender Leny Yoro during Sunday's match.
articles.content: A crucial decision in Sunday's Liverpool vs Manchester United match has been deemed a clear mistake by an independent regulatory commission. The commission found that referee Sam Barrott made an "obvious error when sending off Manchester United defender Leny Yoro. The incident occurred early in the game at Anfield, with Yoro receiving a red card for bringing down Reds striker Alexander Isak as he sprinted towards goal. Debate has been ongoing about whether Isak's heavy touch would have allowed goalkeeper Senne Lammens to reach the ball before him. Referees' chief Howard Webb had initially stated that the decision was certainly not clearly wrong". However, Manchester United lodged an appeal with the Football Association for wrongful dismissal, and their one-match ban was subsequently removed on Tuesday. The independent commission has now published its written reasons, which reveal a unanimous verdict among its members. According to these documents, Yoro's foul would not have given Isak an obvious goalscoring opportunity. Key points highlighted in the commission's ruling include Isak's heavy touch on the ball and his subsequent loss of control, allowing the goalkeeper to intervene. In their view, Lammens would have been able to gather or smother the ball before Isak could shoot at goal. A review of the decision to send off Leny Yoro has led to questions about the referee's judgment during a recent match. The chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, Webb, shared his thoughts on the incident in an interview for the Match Officials: Mic'd Up programme. According to him, there was some uncertainty over whether Isak would reach the ball before Lammens intervened. Webb explained that the referee's decision was based on a split-second assessment of the situation, and it seemed he believed Isak had a good chance of getting to the ball first. The VAR review aimed to determine if this decision was clearly incorrect, but ultimately concluded it wasn't. The independent panel reviewing the incident disagreed with the referee's decision, citing concerns over the validity of certain analysis presented by the club as evidence. The controversy surrounding the sending off of Leny Yoro by referee Barrott during the Liverpool vs Man Utd match has taken a new turn. According to reports, the Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has backed Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' decision not to recommend a review. This development comes as Manchester United Manager Mauricio Pochettino reacts to the sending off of Leny Yoro during the match against Liverpool. The five-person KMI Panel, which includes three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative, and one from Pro Ref, is due to publish its findings for the match week on December 2. The panel's backing of Barrott's decision has sparked further debate about the validity of certain analysis presented by Manchester United as evidence. Despite this, Pro Ref declined to comment on the story or the commission's findings, while Manchester United have been approached for comment but remain silent so far. Manchester United had submitted a video of a challenge by Brighton's Pascal Struijk on Wilson Isidor of Sunderland last month, which led to Struijk being shown a red card after a VAR review. However, an appeal by Brighton led to the suspension being removed, allowing Struijk to return to action and potentially paving the way for Yoro to face Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday. The Red Devils' frustration mounted as Polish referee Szymon Marciniak made several contentious decisions during the match. A potential opening goal for Manchester United was denied after Marciniak blew for what many observers considered a minor infringement by Youri Tielemans, allowing Amad Diallo's shot to be disallowed. The VAR system intervened once more to recommend a review of another incident involving Patrick Dorgu and Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira. The Brazilian appeared to have inadvertently directed the ball into his own net before Dorgu's challenge, but the referee deemed it a foul nonetheless. articles.title: San Antonio Spurs Fall to Trail Blazers in Late-Game Collapse
articles.summary: The San Antonio Spurs' defense imploded in the final seconds, allowing a three-pointer that secured a 116-111 win for the Portland Trail Blazers.
articles.content: The San Antonio Spurs' late-game defense imploded in Portland, allowing a crucial three-pointer to be made and securing a 116-111 win for the Trail Blazers in their NBA Cup matchup. The Spurs had been dominant for most of the game, but Deni Avdija's shot from beyond the arc with just seconds left on the clock turned the tables. This was not the kind of defensive performance the Spurs wanted to showcase, especially considering they had managed to limit the Trail Blazers' scoring opportunities for so long. The 23-second stretch of good defense that preceded Avdija's shot was a rare instance of the team's usually solid defense being breached in such a dramatic fashion. Spurs guard Stephon Castle acknowledged the disappointment of watching that crucial three-pointer drop, saying "It's the NBA, It's the most talented players in the world." We can play 23 seconds of great defense, but they get off a contested 3 and it still gets to drop. The Spurs' offense was unable to overcome a strong showing from the Portland duo of Damian Lillard and Avdija, who combined for impressive performances throughout the game. Lillard's impact was felt immediately as he scored 16 points in the first quarter alone, setting the tone for his team's overall performance. His ability to score effectively early on put pressure on the Spurs' defense from the outset. Avdija made several key contributions down the stretch, including a crucial shot that sealed the win for Portland and sent the Spurs reeling. Despite Castle's efforts to rally his team, Avdija's big shots proved to be too much to overcome. The loss dropped the Spurs to 15-4 on the season, while Portland improved to 12-6 with the victory. The Spurs' loss to Portland has left them tied with three other teams in West Group C pool play, each holding a 2-1 record after three games. A win for San Antonio against Dallas on Friday would secure their spot in the knockout stage, thanks to their significant point differential advantage that will be used as a tiebreaker if needed. Meanwhile, Portland's victory has improved their chances of advancing beyond group stage play, and they can even clinch a wild-card berth with another win over Golden State on Friday. Coach Micah Nori acknowledged his team was given a vote of no confidence in their defensive abilities after he opted to assign 7-foot-2 center to guard Stephon Castle instead of Wembanyama in their previous meeting against the Spurs. The Spurs' high-flying center continued to wreak havoc on opposing defenses, this time in Portland where he found success against the Blazers' big man despite a change in matchups. Wembanyama's ability to adapt and make adjustments on the fly was on full display as he exploited the midrange jumper, a shot that has become a staple of his game. Coach Nori's decision to switch up the lineup seemed to have some effect, but Wembanyama remained a force to be reckoned with, making it clear that he is not easily contained. The Blazers' adjustment helped keep the rest of the Spurs' supporting cast in check, but ultimately proved insufficient against Wembanyama's dominant performance. Wembanyama reflected on his shooting selection after the game, noting that he has been working to improve his shot-making skills and it seems to be paying off. The Spurs' struggles on the road continued, with Vassell's shooting woes a significant contributor to their defeat. His two-game road trip average of 12 shots made from 31 attempts is a concerning trend for the team. Vassell had been out for two games earlier this month due to a groin issue but has since returned to action. However, in the seven games he's played since his return, his field goal percentage has been underwhelming, with only 30 successful shots out of 77 attempts. The Spurs' inability to score consistently is taking its toll on their overall performance, particularly when key players like Dylan Harper and De'Aaron Fox are unavailable. articles.title: Celebrating Thanksgiving in Scotland after nearly two decades abroad
articles.summary: The author, a former study abroad student, grew to appreciate the simplicity and values of Thanksgiving during their time in the US.
articles.content: I made the bold decision to return to Scotland after nearly two decades living in the US, but one tradition has remained steadfast: celebrating Thanksgiving. It all began when I first arrived in the US in 2001 as a study abroad student, and I was perplexed by this peculiar holiday that seemed so deeply ingrained in American culture. But it wasn't long before I grew to appreciate the simplicity of Thanksgiving - the absence of commercialism or religious obligation was refreshing. The idea of taking time out to express gratitude for what one has resonated with me. Celebrating Thanksgiving in Scotland can feel a bit disorienting, but it serves as a vital connection to my life in the US. I've found that embracing this tradition helps me stay rooted in my past while navigating new surroundings. In my early years living in the US, attending Thanksgiving dinners was more of a social obligation than anything else - but as time passed, I began to genuinely appreciate the holiday's spirit and values. As I settled into my new life in Scotland, I found myself missing the sense of community and tradition that had been a big part of my time in the US. Hosting Thanksgiving dinners for friends who were also without family nearby was one way to combat this feeling. I began experimenting with American recipes, adapting them to suit Scottish tastes by adding local ingredients like leeks in cheese sauce, a dish reminiscent of my childhood. My homemade pumpkin cheesecake quickly became an annual request from friends and acquaintances alike. The decision to host Thanksgiving in Scotland wasn't just about recreating a familiar tradition - it also helped me navigate the challenges of rebuilding my life after nearly two decades abroad. Finding a job, securing a new home, and establishing routines were daunting tasks that seemed less overwhelming with something to look forward to. My partner's suggestion to celebrate Thanksgiving was a timely one, as I was struggling to find festive cheer in the shortening days and colder temperatures. His friend from the US, who was feeling homesick at this time of year, also saw the value in hosting an American holiday in Scotland - especially for his two children, who had only experienced it through movies. With a bit of planning, we were able to create a warm and welcoming atmosphere that felt like a true celebration. It was a small but significant way to connect with our community and mark the passing of time in a meaningful way. It's not always easy to get into the Thanksgiving spirit when it feels like the rest of the world is moving on with its daily routine. The first few years after moving back to Scotland from the US were especially challenging. Shopping for ingredients proved to be a bit of an adventure, as some items just weren't readily available in local stores. A can of pumpkin puree, for instance, was nowhere to be found until I stumbled upon it at a health food store - and even then, it came with a hefty price tag of nearly $5 per can. A timely rescue mission by my American friend yielded a bag of fresh cranberries, which helped salvage the shopping trip. Our teenager, usually engrossed in his Rubik's Cube, even took a break to help peel sprouts - although that respite was short-lived. The kids' school friends weren't celebrating Thanksgiving, so our household felt like an oasis of excitement amidst the ordinary routine. After school, the atmosphere shifted, and everyone seemed to be looking forward to the novelty of the holiday. As we sat down to a traditional dinner with all the classics, taking turns to express gratitude was a slightly awkward experience for some guests - but ultimately, it brought everyone together. The sweet potatoes with marshmallows were a sight to behold for my Scottish friends, their faces reflecting a mix of confusion and curiosity as they observed this quintessential American tradition. Despite the initial bewilderment, it soon became apparent that Thanksgiving is a holiday that can transcend cultural boundaries and adapt to different settings. The key lies in its underlying values: gratitude, sharing, and connection with loved ones. For me, Thanksgiving has become a way to stay connected to my American roots, even after living abroad for nearly two decades. It's a tradition that I've managed to incorporate into my new life in Scotland, making it feel like home. In recent years, we've made an effort to observe Thanksgiving on almost every occasion, often hosting small gatherings with our partner and their daughter. However, last year was special, it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, and our tiny apartment became the unlikely venue for a lively celebration. As I rummage through the aisles of Scottish supermarkets in search of essential ingredients, I'm struck by the stark price differences between here and the US. A can of pumpkin puree is now a luxury item that costs more than a gallon of gas back home, a far cry from the abundance we often take for granted in America. After settling back into Scottish life, I discovered ways to adapt Thanksgiving traditions to local ingredients and tastes. For instance, butternut squash or sweet potato puree can substitute for pumpkin in recipes, while red currants or sour cherries offer a cranberry-like flavor. Moving back to Scotland after nearly two decades abroad was not a straightforward process. Leaving behind friends, familiar routines, and the life I had built took some getting used to. However, holding onto Thanksgiving traditions has helped me maintain a connection to my American heritage while building a new life in Scotland. Organizing a mini Turkey Trot before dinner is another way for me to incorporate this tradition into my Scottish home, even if it requires an early morning start. articles.title: Cas12m Protein Family Can Cut DNA After All
articles.summary: A new study has revealed that some members of the Cas12m protein family have an active state capable of cleaving DNA.
articles.content: Researchers at the University of Tokyo have made a groundbreaking discovery about the Cas12m protein family, long considered the "black sheep" of the Cas protein clan due to their inability to cut DNA. Until now, scientists had been puzzled by the fact that these proteins, despite being relatively small and potentially more easily deliverable into cells, were unable to perform the crucial function of cutting DNA. However, a new study has shed light on the structural differences between active and inactive Cas12m variants. The research team, led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga and Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura, found that some Cas12m proteins do indeed have an active state capable of cleaving DNA. This breakthrough opens up new possibilities for developing compact genome-editing tools. These tools could potentially revolutionize biomedical research, medicine, and biotechnology by providing a more efficient and targeted way to edit genes. The study's findings were published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology, offering a significant step forward in understanding the complex world of gene editing. The research team behind the study decided to investigate further whether the lack of DNA cutting ability in some Cas12m proteins was a common trait among all members of this group or if there were still active ones waiting to be discovered. To understand which molecular characteristics contributed to the inactivity of these proteins, the researchers developed a screening system using laboratory bacteria that could test multiple Cas12m candidates and identify those capable of cutting DNA. This allowed them to search for active Cas12m proteins among many potential candidates. The team's efforts paid off as they discovered some Cas12m proteins that were indeed able to cut DNA. However, the researchers still needed to determine what distinguished these active proteins from their inactive counterparts. Using cryo-electron microscopy, a technique that can reveal detailed three-dimensional molecular structures at the atomic scale, the researchers obtained images of both active and inactive Cas12m proteins. Researchers had been trying to pinpoint which amino acids were crucial for Cas12m proteins' ability to cut DNA. Their investigation involved modifying specific amino acids and testing how these changes affected the protein's function. This approach ultimately led them to identify key differences between active and inactive Cas12m variants. The discovery marks a significant milestone in understanding the complex mechanisms governing Cas12m nuclease activation, which is crucial for its application in genome editing. With this knowledge, scientists can now focus on optimizing the performance of these proteins, with the ultimate goal of developing them into practical tools for precise genetic manipulation. articles.title: Octopuses Use Different Strategies to Squeeze Through Gaps
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered that octopuses employ distinct methods to navigate openings of varying sizes, including a four-step process for narrower passages.
articles.content: Researchers at a leading scientific journal have shed light on a previously unknown aspect of octopus behavior: how they squeeze themselves into tiny spaces. According to Wen-Tzu Hsing, lead author of the study, there was a significant knowledge gap in this area before their research began. "There [was] no information about how octopuses squeeze through an opening far smaller than the body diameter," she noted. To investigate, the researchers set up an experimental tank with a transparent acrylic panel and a hole in it. This allowed them to observe the octopus's movement through the gap while keeping the other side visible. The team classified openings as either large or small based on whether they would require the octopus to compress its cartilaginous structure, which protects its central nervous system. They estimated this distance by measuring the space between the octopus's eyes. A significant discovery emerged from this study: octopuses employ different strategies when navigating gaps of varying sizes. When faced with a larger opening, the process involves three distinct steps. The first step is for the octopus to explore the hole using its arms. The researchers observed that before proceeding, the creatures typically insert two arms through the gap on the other side. Only then do they thread their remaining arms and mantle through the opening. The octopuses' strategy for navigating tight spaces involves adapting their approach as the openings become smaller. In cases where the holes are relatively large, they use a combination of arm extension and leverage to squeeze through. However, when faced with narrower passages, they switch to a four-step process that requires more maneuvering. This alternative method begins similarly to the initial approach, with several arms being threaded through the opening. But from there, the octopus employs a distinct series of movements to facilitate its passage. Specifically, it rotates its body upward and pushes the bases of the already-passthrough arms deeper into the hole, effectively widening the passage. The subsequent steps in this four-step process involve twisting and stretching its arms to feed them all through the opening. Once all appendages are on the other side, the octopus slides its head through, leveraging its tentacles on the barrier for added support. This sequence was consistently used by the octopuses when attempting to pass through smaller openings. In 30 observed attempts to navigate a small hole, the octopuses never employed this four-step method when presented with a larger opening. Additionally, side-view footage revealed that during the final step of passing through a narrow opening, the octopus deforms its mantle to reduce its overall diameter and facilitate a smoother passage. The researchers conducting these experiments observed a distinct preference among the octopuses for specific arms when performing each step of their squeezing process. Two species of juvenile octopuses were involved in the study: the common octopus and the Maya octopus, both exhibiting similar behavior in navigating through tight spaces. While the findings may not be universally applicable to all octopus species, the researchers believe that understanding this multi-step process could have significant implications for robotics design, particularly in environments where passageway sizes are unpredictable. The discovery highlights the potential for soft robots to mimic the octopuses' unique ability to adapt and navigate through confined spaces, potentially leading to more effective search and rescue operations. articles.title: South Africa's Cederberg Region Hosts Stargazing Retreats
articles.summary: Guests at Bliss & Stars retreat experience profound transformation during Orion's Odyssey program.
articles.content: The sun's descent behind craggy peaks in South Africa's Cederberg region marked the beginning of a profound transformation for me. The heat-baked sandstone transformed into a deep twilight, enveloping the valley in an eerie silence that seemed to thicken with each passing moment. I had arrived at Bliss & Stars, a secluded retreat perched above the Doring River, specifically for Orion's Odyssey, a program carefully timed to coincide with the new moon. At this time of the month, the sky is at its darkest, and the universe reveals its secrets in breathtaking clarity. The Milky Way's galactic core rose majestically above the ridge as we approached midnight, casting an ethereal glow over the landscape. Its luminous, textured beauty seemed to mirror the flowing reflection of the river below, creating a sense of harmony between the celestial and terrestrial worlds. My phone had lost signal hours earlier on the winding drive into this 3,300-acre private reserve, located deep in the heart of South Africa's Cederberg region. Without a constant stream of notifications and distractions, I was forced to confront my own relationship with technology, a confrontation that initially felt daunting but ultimately rewarding. As I wandered through the darkness, my eyes slowly began to adjust to the absence of artificial light. It takes approximately 20 minutes for our vision to fully adapt to true darkness, and even a single glance at a bright screen can undo this progress. The remote retreat is located on virtually untouched land that was acquired by the owners in 2019. To make the lodge accessible, they first had to construct a rudimentary access road before building could begin. The construction process required transporting materials by pickup truck and trailer, which were then carried by hand for the final stretch. The chalets are strategically positioned between boulders or nestled into the rock face above the river, offering guests an immersive experience with nature. In recent years, a villa was added to the existing units, increasing the total number of accommodations to six and allowing up to 10 guests at a time. Each evening, participants in the stargazing retreats gather on a circular viewing deck in front of the observatory for dinner and some relaxation before gazing at the stars. Heine takes charge of these nighttime sessions, using them as an opportunity to lead his guests on guided star meditations. These meditations are designed to dislodge rather than ground participants, taking them on what Heine calls a "little mental space walk." During this exercise, he invites listeners to release stress and anxiety by breathing in the night air through their noses and exhaling slowly. As the meditation progresses, gravity seems to lose its hold, leaving guests feeling as if they might float. At the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, Heine offers a guided tour of the night sky without using technical jargon. He finds a nebula and walks his small group through it, allowing them to take turns peering into the eyepiece for a closer look at the celestial wonder. The lodge's guest list is a diverse one, comprising individuals from all walks of life who share a common goal: to disconnect from the world and reconnect with themselves. They come seeking purpose, looking for answers, or simply wanting to escape the chaos they left behind. Heine delves into the concept of time, revealing that moonlight takes approximately one second to reach us after leaving the moon's surface. In contrast, sunlight takes around eight minutes to travel from the sun and reach our planet. This seemingly trivial detail sparks a deeper exploration of the universe's vastness. The evening sky is filled with celestial wonders, including two satellite galaxies, the Magellanic Clouds, which are visible in the southern hemisphere. Their light has been traveling through space for over 160,000 years, a testament to the age and history of our galaxy. This astronomical fact serves as a reminder that our existence is but a small part of the universe's grand tapestry. During one of the morning sessions, Daria introduces the group to ceremonial cacao, a rich and warm beverage designed to prepare the nervous system for what lies ahead. While it may not be a substitute for coffee, this traditional medicine has its own unique properties that help guests transition into their day. The Cederberg landscape is a reminder that even the most profound concerns can be put into perspective by the sheer vastness of nature. To allow oneself to feel and process emotions, one must first make room for them in their daily life, Daria emphasizes during morning breathwork sessions. Stress manifests itself in various ways, including shallow breathing and clenched jaws, as observed by Daria in her work with guests like myself. The shared experience of releasing pent-up emotions brought unexpected moments of catharsis to our small group, ranging from laughter to tears. As we ventured out after brunch, the landscape revealed its secrets: Cape mountain leopard tracks pressed into the sand and raptors soaring overhead in search of thermal currents. The meals at this retreat were surprisingly indulgent despite adhering to a strict diet of vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Buddha bowls and ancient grain salads made up a significant portion of our dining experience, while roasted vegetables added a satisfying crunch to each meal. One evening, after a hike into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, we were treated to an introduction to astrophotography by Heine, one of the retreat's facilitators. The process of capturing light involved holding a shutter open long enough for it to gather photons that had been traveling through space for centuries. Standing still in complete darkness with only a torch under my chin, I managed to take a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, with the camera collecting and recording these ancient photons. On our final night at the retreat, the telescope and dinner were perfectly synchronized, allowing us to gaze up at the stars while enjoying a six-course meal. The nights at Bliss & Stars were long and dark, perfect for stargazing during our summer visit. The sky turned inky black after midnight, making it an ideal time to gaze up at the stars. This was a deliberate choice by the retreat's hosts, who catered to the natural rhythms of their guests. As I settled into my chalet's bed, I sipped on a soothing drink made from locally grown rooibos tea and wildflower honey from a flask. The unique mattress, filled with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, proved to be a comfortable resting place for the night. The floor-to-ceiling windows, without curtains, allowed the morning light to flood in and gently wake me up. The absence of curtains was a deliberate design choice, meant to reset one's circadian rhythm in harmony with nature. As I opened my eyes during the small hours, I was met with an unforgettable sight: the night sky framed by the glass windows. It was a breathtaking view that left a lasting impression on me. articles.title: Pilgrims' Traditional Harvest Celebrations Were Not Uniquely American
articles.summary: Historical records show that harvest celebrations were common in early America, with no evidence of a direct link between the first Thanksgiving and modern-day celebrations.
articles.content: The traditional American holiday of Thanksgiving is being reevaluated for its origins. The notion that it has been celebrated in a uniform way since the early days of European settlement is a myth. In reality, the first Thanksgiving was just one of many harvest celebrations held by the Pilgrims and their neighbors. While children often learn about the 1621 feast as if it were a singular event, historical records indicate that seasonal food such as venison, corn, and turkeys were likely on the menu. However, there is no clear evidence to suggest that these foods have remained staples of American Thanksgiving celebrations over time. The idea of a direct line connecting the "first Thanksgiving to modern-day celebrations is an American narrative created in the 19th century. This myth was designed to unite the nation and facilitate the assimilation of new immigrants, rather than accurately represent historical facts. The Pilgrims' tradition of holding fasts and feasts continued after their arrival in Massachusetts, with some governors declaring fall holidays of thanksgiving. However, these celebrations were not coordinated across colonies or states, highlighting the diversity of early American harvest traditions. Sarah Josepha Hale's vision for a unified American holiday began to take shape in the 1830s when she became the editor of Godey's Lady's Book. This influential magazine was a staple in many households, boasting the largest circulation of any U.S. publication before the Civil War. Hale's editorial efforts focused on promoting homemakers as the backbone of American society, responsible for fostering wholesome families and contributing to the nation's identity. Her vision for a national Thanksgiving holiday aimed to unite Americans across different regions and backgrounds under one common celebration. Godey's Lady's Book played a pivotal role in shaping the early traditions of American Thanksgiving, providing readers with recipes, decorating ideas, and even editorials advocating for a unified national holiday. The magazine's influence was far-reaching, helping to popularize seasonal dishes like turkey and cranberry sauce. As the Industrial Revolution took hold, Hale recognized the importance of unpaid domestic labor, which was often overlooked in favor of factory work. Her vision for Thanksgiving celebrated the contributions of homemakers, highlighting their role as guardians of family values and national identity. Hale's vision for Thanksgiving wasn't just about family gatherings; it also highlighted the role of homemakers as guardians of national identity. Her petition to five presidents eventually paid off when Abraham Lincoln declared Thanksgiving a national holiday, hoping that it would unite the country during the Civil War. In support of the troops, Northern women sent care packages with pies and turkeys, while abolitionist Sojourner Truth collected funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners for African American soldiers. The adoption of Thanksgiving as a national holiday was a gradual process, influenced by various factors such as Protestant traditions, regional differences, and social changes like industrialization and urbanization. As the country adjusted to these transformations, Godey's Lady's Book played a significant role in shaping the way Americans celebrated Thanksgiving, connecting the holiday menu to the nation's past and inspiring resilience in the face of change. The concept of Thanksgiving as a unifying force in American society took hold, and it wasn't long before the holiday was seen as an opportunity to integrate immigrants into the nation's fabric. This notion gained traction through the works of political cartoonist Thomas Nast, whose illustration Uncle Sam's Thanksgiving Dinner published in Harper's Weekly in 1869 depicted a diverse group of Americans from various racial and ethnic backgrounds seated together at a table, surrounded by portraits of presidents. The image sent a clear message that immigrants could be fully incorporated into the nation. The timing of Nast's cartoon was significant, coming just one year after the passage of the 14th Amendment, which granted citizenship to anyone born in the United States, and four years after the abolition of slavery as stipulated by the 13th Amendment. This marked a crucial juncture in American history, with the nation grappling with issues of identity and belonging. The sentiment expressed in Nast's illustration stood in stark contrast to a similar cartoon created eight years later by G.F. Keller for the San Francisco Wasp, which portrayed a group of disheveled men from different nationalities eating their respective traditional foods, reinforcing the notion that immigrants could never truly assimilate into American culture. In public schools across America, children were taught about the significance of Thanksgiving, often returning home with recipe cards featuring traditional dishes that had been popularized by Sarah Hale in the previous century. These lessons framed the Pilgrims as a symbol of American identity, portraying them as the first immigrants to set foot on the continent. However, this narrative glossed over the complexities of the Pilgrims' arrival, which more closely resembled colonization than immigration. As Thanksgiving became an integral part of public school curricula by the 1920s, it served as a means of inclusivity for newcomers. Immigrant children were able to connect with their own heritage through the celebration, seeing parallels between their own experiences and those of the Pilgrims. For Jewish immigrants, the holiday presented an opportunity to adapt traditional dishes to fit their cultural and dietary needs. The introduction of Crisco as a nondairy butter substitute in the early 1900s allowed them to create unique American" desserts that were both festive and kosher-friendly. By embracing Thanksgiving with their own twists, immigrant families found ways to make the holiday their own, often blending traditional dishes with American classics to create something uniquely theirs. The traditional Thanksgiving celebration in America has been shaped by various cultural influences over time. Immigrant families found ways to incorporate their own traditions into the holiday, often blending familiar dishes with American classics to create unique and personalized celebrations. This blending of cultures was made possible by the fact that most families traditionally celebrate Thanksgiving at home, allowing newcomers to participate in the national culture while still expressing their own heritage. As a result, diverse culinary traditions have become an integral part of the holiday, reflecting the melting pot nature of American society.
